claim: According to his family, Jafar Sardar (35) of Bara Meghla village, Jashore Sadar, left home on 17 August 2024 bound for Cyprus through a Dhaka agency named 'Dream Home Travels', which had submitted his papers to the Cyprus embassy; when no visa came in two years it took him to Saudi Arabia with talk of a job in Russia, and two months later he was taken to Russia through Dubai, Libya or Turkey.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025 stated that 84,000 Bangladeshis went to Europe by sea from 2009 to 2024 and that on average at least 100 Bangladeshis die each year when boats sink (it gives no source for either figure).
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
why_new: A Bangladeshi death estimate per year; the guide gives only all-nationality deaths. Unsourced in the article, so needs a source before use.

claim: According to CID information cited in a Prothom Alo editorial of 1 April 2026, 17,000 Bangladeshis were sent to Italy by illegal routes in the previous year.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
why_new: A CID figure for the year to March 2026; differs from the 20,164 sea arrivals for 2025 the section already gives, so note the source.

claim: By the ambassador's account, about two-thirds of the 113 returnees on that flight identified themselves as from Madaripur.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
why_new: How concentrated the route is in one district, from a head count on a return flight.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme, said on 18 April 2026 that Bangladeshis are the largest group in the world crossing the Mediterranean to Europe, a situation that has lasted a decade, and that people from 8 to 10 districts, among them Madaripur, Shariatpur, Sylhet, Sunamganj and Habiganj, are losing their lives going this way.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
why_new: The source districts, named by BRAC; the guide gives no district list for the boat route.

claim: The general secretary of the Sylhet District Press Club said on 18 April 2026 that over the previous 10 years at least 10,000 people had died or gone missing, more than two and a half lakh had been trafficked abroad by illegal routes and at least 15,000 had been jailed in various countries (he gave no source).
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
why_new: Ten-year totals from a speaker with no source given; usable only with attribution or after checking.

claim: The Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime unit identified a Libya-based trafficker who had appointed 40 brokers across Bangladesh whose job was to find young people wanting to go abroad, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: Shows the scale of one Libya-based trafficker's recruiting network in Bangladesh (40 brokers).

claim: Azmir Hossain said he reached Dubai on 21 March 2024, where the broker's men met him at the airport and kept 30 to 35 people together in a room of a small house for two days, then flew them to Egypt, held them 24 hours in a warehouse-like place in the airport area, and put them on another plane to Libya.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: Stop-by-stop detail of the Dubai and Egypt legs: who meets them, how many per room, how long at each.

claim: The boat crossing from Libya to Europe is known as the 'game'; small boats are mainly used and are loaded beyond capacity, Prothom Alo wrote in February 2025.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: The guide uses 'game houses' without saying that the crossing itself is called the 'game'.

claim: According to relatives, police and local sources, the two Rajoir men left home on 1 January 2025, flew from Dhaka through Dubai to Libya, were sent by the broker to the coast, and left the Libyan coast on an engine boat on 24 January.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: Timing: 23 days from leaving home in Madaripur to the boat.

claim: The 24 Shariatpur and Madaripur men were sent first to the United Arab Emirates, then through Egypt to Libya, according to Palong Model police station and relatives.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: Confirms the UAE-Egypt-Libya routing for 2022-24 departures from Shariatpur.

claim: Md Touhid Hossain, the former foreign affairs adviser, wrote in April 2026 that because surveillance and restrictions on the route to Italy had recently increased, traffickers were now using the Greece route.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: A named former official on the 2026 shift from Italy to Greece as the destination from Libya.

claim: Md Touhid Hossain wrote that the main route to Italy by sea used to be a flight to Kenya, then overland to Libya, then the boat, and that a person boards the plane to Kenya on a false story of a safari or tourism; along the way people change hands several times like goods.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
why_new: A Kenya entry point and the cover story used at departure; the guide's path lists only Dubai, Egypt, India and Sri Lanka.

claim: On 15 February 2024 a boat carrying 52 migrants caught fire and sank in the Mediterranean off the Tunisian coast; 8 Bangladeshis died, 26 others were rescued and one was seriously injured, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: The February 2024 Tunisia boat deaths are not in the Death list.

claim: According to relatives, police and local sources, several young men from Rajoir, Madaripur, and Muksudpur, Gopalganj, left home for Italy on 14 January 2024, flew through Dubai to Libya, and on 14 February left Libya on an engine boat through brokers; eight of them died on the boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia (five from Rajoir and three from Muksudpur), along with one Pakistani.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Home districts, dates and route of the February 2024 Tunisia boat deaths.

claim: Relatives of the eight dead told journalists at Dhaka airport on 2 May 2024 that brokers had put 52 people on a small boat that could take 30, that the eight who died had been forced to stay below the deck, and that when they tried to come out for lack of oxygen the brokers beat them and sent them back down; the relatives said they died of the torture and lack of oxygen.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: How people die on these boats without the boat sinking: overloading and being held below deck.

claim: Azmir Hossain said everyone's passport was taken as soon as they reached Libya, that he was beaten whenever he mentioned the promised job, and that BDT 6 lakh was collected from his family in stages by phone.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A survivor's first-person account of what follows arrival.

claim: Azmir Hossain said that after collecting BDT 6 lakh from his family the broker sold him to another group at a high price and left him in a Libyan desert to be handed over; he said he escaped with a Libyan citizen's help and took shelter with a Bangladeshi he knew, and that the broker then came and took him back.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Being sold on after the ransom is paid, by the same Bangladeshi who recruited him.

claim: Azmir Hossain said he was locked in a room and beaten regularly for trying to escape, went eight days without food, and reached home on 5 May 2024 in a critical condition, 41 days after leaving home according to Prothom Alo; his mother said he is now mentally ill from blows to the head and that she owes BDT 6 lakh.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: The whole trip lasted 41 days and never left Libya; the outcome for the family.

claim: Prothom Alo reported on 13 July 2024 that at least 24 people from Bhairab and elsewhere in Kishoreganj, Habiganj and Narsingdi went to Libya at about the same time through a broker ring led by Rasel Mia of Bhairab to cross to Italy by sea, that none had reached Italy, and that some were hostages of kidnappers and others were in Libyan jails.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A whole batch from one broker stranded; two outcomes, kidnappers or Libyan jail.

claim: Families of two hostages in the Bhairab case said in July 2024 that large ransoms were being demanded but that they could find no one who could assure them that paying would get the men released.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Families' own statement that nobody guarantees release after payment.

claim: According to local people in Bhairab, when the hostages phoned home begging to be freed, the broker Rasel Mia and his ring members hid and cut off contact with the families; the families then went to community leaders for a remedy and got no result.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: What the local broker does once people are taken hostage, and that village arbitration failed.

claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 September 2024 that a broker ring sent 26 young men from 25 families in Goalnagar union, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, and Ratani village, Austagram, Kishoreganj, to Libya on the promise of Italy, each paying BDT 11 lakh; nine came home after torture and harassment, some of the rest were captive and several were missing.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A village cluster case with the outcome counted: 9 of 26 back, none in Italy.

claim: Returnees from Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, and Austagram, Kishoreganj, said that two and a half to three months after the last payment the broker sold them, that after three months in jail they reached their families through a Pakistani man with the help of a man from Bhairab, and could come home only after each paid a further BDT 1 lakh 20 thousand for the air ticket and other costs; they returned between 7 August and 14 September 2024 after release from Libyan jail.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Getting out of Libyan jail and home cost each man a further BDT 1.2 lakh, paid by the family.

claim: Suman Mia of Nasirnagar told Prothom Alo he paid the broker BDT 11 lakh in all and was told he would be taken to Italy within a week; he said 60 people were put on a boat from Benghazi, and after it had run for an hour they understood they had all been sold.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A 'boat to Italy' that was in fact the handover to buyers.

claim: Suman Mia said the 60 were held in a camp for a month and a half, beaten every day and fed once in 24 hours, given two litres of salt water for bathing and the toilet and one bread at night, and made to do cleaning work from morning to evening at the house of a man named Ahammad, whose son beat them with a pistol when they did not work.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Conditions and forced unpaid labour in the camp, in a survivor's words.

claim: Enamul Haque of Lalurtuk village, Nasirnagar, said he spent BDT 22 lakh to send two sons (land sold for BDT 7 lakh, a BDT 12 lakh loan and savings), that one son was 'sold four times', and that he last spoke to the other a year earlier; both were missing in September 2024.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Repeated resale of one person (four times), and disappearance for a year.

claim: The wife of one Mathbaria hostage refused to name the brokers to Prothom Alo in January 2025, saying she wanted her husband back, and the family of another refused to speak at all, believing someone known to the brokers lived near their home and that the torture would increase if word got out.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Why families stay silent while a relative is held: the ring has eyes in the village.

claim: According to the Bangladesh embassy in Libya, a boat carrying 56 people trying to reach Italy from Libya sank in the Mediterranean on 25 January 2025 and 23 bodies washed up on the beach between 28 and 31 January; the bodies were decomposed and not formally identified, but the embassy, citing local sources, said nearly all were Bangladeshi.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: The January 2025 sinking (23 bodies) is not in the Death list.

claim: The father of Hridoy Howlader of Kamarkhali, Faridpur, said the group was to be taken to Italy by ship on the night of 24 January 2025, that many refused to board when a small boat was offered instead, and that those who refused were shot dead while those who boarded drowned, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A family's allegation that people who refused the small boat were shot; the guide has no account of forced boarding.

claim: According to relatives and police, 24 young men from Shariatpur and Madaripur who were taken from home in 2022 and 2023 to be sent to Italy from Libya by an illegal route went missing in Libya; relatives claim none of the 24 has contacted family since 21 and 22 March 2024.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A batch of 24 from one broker lost on the same two days with no word for 11 months.

claim: Riaz Akon said his family gave the broker BDT 20 lakh, raised by selling land and a cattle farm, to send his younger brother to Italy, had had no trace of him for a year, and that the broker gave no information when asked.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A second family's payment and the broker's silence.

claim: According to Rasel Mia's family, the ring demanded BDT 10 lakh more a few days before his death, and when the family could not pay he was tortured and died in Libya on 21 February 2025; the family learned of the death the next day through an expatriate, and his father, who said he had paid BDT 50 lakh in stages by selling his homestead and farmland, alleged his son was killed with a poisonous injection.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Death after the family ran out of money, having paid BDT 50 lakh; guide's Death list has boats only, plus the two contract-price cases.

claim: Khurshed Mia said that in Libya, after a month without work, he got a job at a shopping mall 'in exchange for 500 dinars' that was to pay 1,400 dinars at the end of the month but paid him half, and then worked four months at an oil company for 1,200 dinars a month.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: What work in Libya paid in 2024, the fee to get a job, and wage theft.

claim: Khurshed Mia said law-enforcement officers raided the fourth-floor flat where 11 of them lived at about 1:30 am on 10 July 2024 and he hid for two hours on the window ledge; later he was kept in a place with 210 other people, where a raid at 10 pm took away 160 while he hid for four hours in a tree.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Raids by Libyan forces on migrants' housing and on a holding house of over 200 people.

claim: Khurshed Mia said a mafia group attacked the building the broker had moved him to and he jumped from the first floor to save himself, injuring his arm and leg; he got no treatment for five days, the broker's men moved him from a private hospital to a government hospital because they could not bear the cost, he had five operations in three and a half months there, and he came home on 13 February 2025 unable to walk.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Permanent disability as an outcome, and what medical care looked like for an injured migrant in Libya.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 1 April 2026 said the family of Shayek Ahmed (23) of Sunamganj gave brokers BDT 12 lakh by selling their cows and land, that the rubber boat he left on from Libya for Greece on 21 March lost its way and drifted for six days, that he died of starvation when the food ran out, and that 12 young men from Sunamganj died on that journey and their bodies were thrown into the sea.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Adds to the March 2026 Greece boat already in the Death list: rubber boat, six days adrift, death by starvation, 12 of the dead from Sunamganj, price paid.

claim: Returnees told the ambassador to Libya before their flight home in spring 2026 that one had eaten rice once after twenty days, five men sharing one bowl with no curry, that another got a handful after twenty-five days, and that a piece of bread was thrown at them 'the way food is given to a dog' and they were beaten as well.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Detainees' own words on food in captivity.

claim: On 4 April 2026 a wooden boat that left Tajoura, Libya, for the Italian island of Lampedusa with about 105 passengers sank; 32 people were rescued alive and 2 bodies recovered, the other 71 were missing, and Bangladeshis were among both the rescued and the missing, Md Touhid Hossain wrote in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: The April 2026 Tajoura sinking is not in the Death list; names Tajoura as a departure point.

claim: Md Touhid Hossain wrote in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026 that a boat that left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026 with 48 passengers drifted for six days before 26 people were rescued alive, 21 of them Bangladeshis, and that 20 of the 22 dead or missing were reported to be Bangladeshi.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Different counts from the guide's for the same March 2026 boat (guide: 43 aboard, 38 Bangladeshis, at least 18 dead); record the conflict.

claim: Md Touhid Hossain wrote that many Bengalis are among those who torture the hostages in Libya, and that the people who collect ransom from families in Bangladesh by showing torture videos live undisturbed in the same society.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A former foreign adviser stating that Bangladeshis do the torturing and the ransom collection is done at home.

claim: Mizanur Rahman said that, still not released after the payments and seeing how severe the torture was, he broke a window, escaped and gave himself up to Libyan police, and later came home in 2026 through IOM; eleven people tortured by the same ring came home from Libya through IOM in 2026 and joined the human chain.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A way out that worked: escaping and surrendering to Libyan police, then return through IOM.

claim: At the same human chain, Taslima Begum said her husband Habib was killed because the family could not pay a ransom of BDT 10 lakh; she now lives with their three children at her father's house.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A killing alleged over an unpaid BDT 10 lakh ransom.

claim: According to investigators, on 5 August 2025 the wife of Md Saiful (39) of Sundarganj, Gaibandha, who had gone to Libya about two years before November 2026 through a Bangladeshi broker, got a call from a Libyan mobile number saying he was in the callers' custody, that BDT 30 lakh ransom must be paid or he would be killed, and that no one in the family would be allowed to speak to him until half the ransom was paid.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: A ransom demand with no proof of life: half must be paid before the family may hear the man's voice.

claim: The CID said the family sent BDT 5 lakh in all between 10 and 25 August 2025 from a bKash shop at Bamandanga Hall Mor, Sundarganj, to several mobile numbers the accused gave, and that even after the money was received the family was not put in touch with Saiful.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: How ransom is paid inside Bangladesh: mobile-wallet transfers from a local agent shop to several numbers.

claim: According to the CID, the father of the Gaibandha hostage was then contacted from another number and asked for a further BDT 42 lakh in the name of rescuing his son, and was told his son was held by two men in Libya named Mokarram and Anwar from whom the caller had got the father's number; the father said he would pay nothing more unless he could speak to his son directly, and no more calls came to him or to his son's wife.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
why_new: Successive callers demanding rising sums (30, then 42 lakh) with no proof of life; when the family insisted on speaking to him, the calls stopped.

claim: A union parishad member in Karerhat, Mirsarai, said he phoned the Libya-based broker several times to get Azmir Hossain sent home and saw the marks of beating on Azmir's head and body on a video call.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
why_new: An elected local representative negotiating directly with the broker in Libya, and a witness to the injuries.

claim: The Deputy Commissioner of Pirojpur, asked in January 2025 about three local men held for ransom in Libya, said the administration has little it can do in such cases, but that if the family complains it can inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in writing.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
why_new: What a district administration says it can actually do for a hostage's family: forward a written complaint to the Foreign Ministry.

claim: On 15 February 2025, on hearing of the arrest, relatives of the missing men began a hunger strike in the grounds of the Shariatpur District and Sessions Judge's court demanding exemplary punishment and the tracing of the missing men.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
why_new: Arrest did not produce information on the missing; families resorted to a hunger strike.

claim: The 113 migrants reached Dhaka the next day, and IOM paid the whole cost from the airfare to their travel back to their own villages, Md Touhid Hossain wrote in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026; they went home with nothing.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
why_new: Says exactly what IOM covers on a return flight: airfare and onward travel to the village.

claim: The father of the Gaibandha hostage filed a case under the trafficking Act at Sundarganj police station on 5 September 2025, the case was sent to the CID for investigation, and on 12 November 2026 the CID arrested two men from Chandpur village, Singra, at Singra Bazar, Natore; the CID said it was still gathering information on where in Libya the son was held and on rescuing him.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
why_new: A second example of a family's police case reaching the CID and producing arrests, here 14 months after filing, with the hostage still not found.

claim: In its statement on the Gaibandha case on 13 November 2026 the CID asked everyone to verify the legality of the person, the agency, the visa and the employing firm before going abroad.
target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
why_new: The CID's stated advice (it does not say how to verify).

claim: Faridul Alam of Chandanaish, Chattogram, who had worked in Dubai since 2003, told a columnist writing in Prothom Alo in December 2024 that he made a verbal contract of BDT 5 lakh with a Bangladeshi broker from Noakhali to be taken as far as Greece: BDT 50,000 in advance, BDT 1.5 lakh after reaching Iran and the remaining BDT 3 lakh after reaching Turkey.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: A stage-payment contract tied to borders crossed (advance, Iran, Turkey) on a route the guide does not cover.

claim: By Faridul Alam's account, at the end of 2010 the smugglers put him and several others in a taxi in Dubai that crossed the UAE border into a coastal hill area of Oman though the passengers had no passport or visa, and from there about thirty young men were put on a boat to Bandar Abbas in Iran, where another Bangladeshi broker received them.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: First legs of the Gulf-to-Greece route: Dubai, Oman by taxi, boat to Bandar Abbas.

claim: By Faridul Alam's account, after he reached Iran a relative in Dubai deposited BDT 1.5 lakh into an Iranian bank account the brokers gave, and the balance of the contract was paid into a bank account the brokers gave while the group was held in Istanbul.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: How the stage payments are collected: bank accounts supplied by the brokers in the transit country.

claim: Faridul Alam said the group was kept about seven days in Iran and taken by taxi and then bus into Turkey, that police took them off the bus on the way to Istanbul and sent them back to the border six times, and that the broker's men sent them again each time until they reached Istanbul on the seventh attempt.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: Iran-Turkey leg, with six failed attempts inside Turkey.

claim: Faridul Alam said that in Istanbul many people were kept crammed in one room and not allowed outside for more than a month, and that about a hundred people were then loaded for Greece into a closed lorry-like vehicle with room for 25 to 30 at most.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: Holding house in Istanbul and the overloaded closed lorry across the Greek border.

claim: By Faridul Alam's account, Greek soldiers or border guards caught the group where the lorry dropped them and put them in jail, UN refugee agency staff then moved them to a refugee camp, and after about ten days they were given a document called a 'stay paper' and took a bus to Athens with the EUR 60 per person the smugglers had handed them in Istanbul.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: What arrival in Greece looked like on this route.

claim: Faridul Alam said he presented himself as Rohingya in all his asylum applications in Greece because the smuggling ring's brokers advised that asylum might be easier that way; the court did not accept his application and stamped his stay paper, which let him stay one month, and he never got asylum in Greece despite four or five interviews.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: Brokers coaching a false nationality for asylum, and that it did not work.

claim: Faridul Alam said he lived about four years in Athens hawking and doing manual work, with police at times detaining him and taking his goods, and that what he earned fed him and left nothing to send to his family in Bangladesh.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: The economic outcome: no remittance after reaching Europe.

claim: Faridul Alam's asylum applications were rejected in Germany, where he lived on EUR 350 a month from a refugee camp from 2015 to 2018, and again in Paris, where the process took from 2018 to 2021; in December 2024 he was cooking for a mess of Bangladeshis in La Courneuve, Paris.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: Fourteen years after leaving Dubai: three countries' asylum refusals and no legal status.

claim: Faridul Alam said the Bangladesh embassy in Paris took his application and fingerprints for a passport and, after a long wait, told him it could not issue a new passport unless he submitted his old Bangladeshi one, which he had thrown away when he set out from Dubai because, he said, an asylum application cannot be made while holding it.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: The cost of destroying the passport for an asylum claim: he cannot get a new one to go home.

claim: Sujan Mia of Simtola village, Chhatak upazila, said on 18 April 2026 that he first went from Bangladesh to Oman for construction work, moved to Dubai after a problem with his iqama (residence permit) and then worked in Qatar, and later returned to Dubai to head for Europe, going through Oman to Iran, Turkey, Greece, North Macedonia and Serbia, working illegally to survive.
target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
why_new: A second, later account of the Dubai-Oman-Iran-Turkey-Greece route, supporting a section for it.

claim: From 21 January 2026, Bangladeshi citizens approved for a US business or tourist visa (B1/B2) must post a bond of up to USD 15,000, the US Embassy in Dhaka said in a notice on its verified Facebook page on 19 January 2026, and the condition does not apply to holders of valid B1/B2 visas issued before that date; Prothom Alo put USD 15,000 at about Tk 18 lakh 35 thousand at Tk 122.31 a dollar.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: A new, large payment tied to a US visitor visa that the guide does not mention.

claim: The US State Department's travel website said on 6 January 2026 that citizens of 38 countries including Bangladesh must post a visa bond of up to USD 15,000 when applying to enter the United States, and the embassy's notice said the bond money is returned if the visa's conditions are properly followed.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: Scope of the bond and the refund condition.

claim: The US Embassy in Dhaka said in a Facebook post on 26 January 2026 that an applicant found eligible after the visa interview is given payment instructions by the consular officer with a direct link to pay.gov, and must pay the bond within 30 days.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: Says how and where the genuine payment is made (only after the interview, on the link the consular officer gives), which is the check against a fake payment site.

claim: Under the visa bond pilot programme the visa issued is single-entry and valid for at most three months, the holder must enter the United States through certain designated ports of entry, and the bond is cancelled automatically and the money returned after the holder comes home if all the visa's conditions are met, among them not working in the United States and returning within the set time, the embassy said.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: The conditions under which the bond is lost: working in the US or overstaying.

claim: In a column in Prothom Alo on 27 March 2026, Dr Delwar Arif, an associate professor at Canisius University in New York, wrote that according to reports aired by ABC's Channel 7, MSN and Bangla channels in the United States, a Bangladeshi in New York who posed as an immigration lawyer without being one, and his firm, took millions of dollars from Bangladeshi and other legal and illegal immigration-seekers in the United States, USD 60 thousand from one person alone.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: A fake-immigration-lawyer fraud against Bangladeshis already in the US; a pattern the guide lacks. Source is an opinion column citing US media, so weaker than a news report.

claim: The same column says the ring also took crores of taka from thousands of people in the name of sending them to the United States, through well-furnished offices in upmarket areas of Dhaka and eye-catching advertisements.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: Shows the Dhaka end: a smart office and advertising as the lure.

claim: According to the column, the fraudsters' advertisements say "Do you want to settle in America?" (আপনি কি আমেরিকায় স্থায়ী হতে চান?) and "Get a green card in America by investing only Tk 50 to 60 lakh"; the writer says they take Tk 50 to 60 lakh a head only to bring a person across the southern or northern border of the United States, and that the dalals and traffickers do not care what happens after arrival or whether the person is caught.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: The exact advertising lines and the price, with what is actually delivered (a border crossing, not a green card).

claim: The columnist writes that in his nearly two decades in the United States he has heard of many cases of people being cheated through Bangladeshi immigration lawyers, that many highly educated Bangladeshis are among the victims, and that US embassies could protect would-be migrants through public awareness campaigns and joint work with local law enforcement.
target_section: NEW: The United States
why_new: Who gets caught (including the educated); opinion of a named academic.

claim: A US Embassy official filed a case at Gulshan police station, Dhaka, on the Monday before 14 February 2024 against five Bangladeshis on charges of involvement in human trafficking; the case says two of them, Mofizur Rahman (54) and Ashraful Alam Bhuiyan (33), went for US visa interviews on 11 February and admitted during the interviews that they are involved in trafficking people from Bangladesh to various countries and work mainly as dalals.
target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
why_new: An embassy itself filing a trafficking case after a visa interview; not in the guide.

claim: According to CJI and Documented's analysis of US Customs and Border Protection records, border crossings from Bangladesh rose 150% from 2019 to 2024; Noakhali is the top district of origin, with more than 30% of the Bangladeshis detained at the border, and Feni is among the top 10 Bangladeshi towns from which people reached the US-Mexico border.

why_new: Growth of the route and the home districts. The data record birthplace, not last residence, and about 35% of records leave birthplace blank, by the article's own account.
